items.rationale: The script's own call order fixes every step, so code owns the control flow. Picking a model-chosen next step (a or b) means the model owns it, even if the prompt lists the allowed steps.

When the order is known and never varies, letting the model choose it adds a model call per decision and run-to-run variation for no gain. Options a and b are false, and c is a risk that a fixed order avoids but not the main reason.

Which lookup comes next depends on what the previous one found, so no fixed sequence can be written in advance; that is where a model-directed loop earns its cost. Free text, many tools and written output are all handled inside fixed workflows too.

items.answer: The code should own the order, because the steps and their order are the same for every booking.

items.rationale: The sequence is known and identical each time, with only a branch on free or busy, so a fixed workflow with a model used just for reading the message and phrasing the reply is cheaper and more predictable. Answering that the model should own the order shows the belief that anything involving a model should be an agent.

Only the questions that need a variable number of fetches need model-chosen steps, so give the model that control in that branch and keep the rest fixed. A bigger model or better labels do not give the fixed path an extra fetch, and rebuilding everything pays agent cost on the easy questions.

Code owns the outer order and the cap, but the model owns how many searches happen, so the design is a mix. Worst case is 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 calls, so the cost has a ceiling, but a request that finishes after one search costs less.
